Last chapter's whole lesson was: do not stand at the counter asking the same question over and over. But that raises an obvious problem. What if Mara genuinely needs to know the _moment_ a new order lands, not next Monday, but now, so she can pack a fragile piece before the buyer changes their mind about the shipping address?

The patient, once-and-remember approach says "check every so often." But if she wants to know _right away_ , checking every so often means either asking constantly (rude, and rate-limited) or missing the moment (checked at 2:00, order came at 2:01, found it at 3:00). There is a tension here between "don't ask too often" and "know right away," and it feels unresolvable.

It is resolved by turning the whole thing around. Instead of Mara's pipeline knocking on the shop's door asking "anything new? anything new?", the shop rings _Mara's_ doorbell the instant something happens. She stops asking. She waits to be told. That reversal is one of the most elegant ideas in this whole territory, and it has a friendly name that matches the picture exactly: a webhook, a doorbell.


### 8.1 Knocking versus being rung

Let us name the two ways to learn that something happened, because the choice between them is a real judgment call you will make often.

The first way is **knocking** : your pipeline goes to the counter window every so often and asks, "has anything changed since last time?" Most of the time the answer is "no," and the visit was wasted. Ask too seldom and you learn about the change late. Ask too often and you are the impolite visitor from Chapter 7. Knocking is simple and it always works, but it is a compromise between freshness and courtesy, and you cannot have both.

The second way is **being rung** : you give the service a way to reach _you_ , and it promises to contact you the moment the thing you care about happens. Now you ask nothing at all. You go about your day, and when a new order lands, the shop reaches out and says, unprompted, "a new order just arrived, here it is." No wasted visits, no delay, no rudeness. The freshness-versus-courtesy compromise dissolves, because you are no longer the one asking.


#### Definition: A webhook (the doorbell)

A **webhook** is an arrangement where a service, instead of waiting to be asked, _reaches out to you_ the moment a particular event happens, and delivers the news, often as a little box of JSON describing what occurred. You register, in effect, an address where the service can reach you and a list of events you care about, and from then on the service rings that doorbell whenever one of those events occurs. The name was coined in 2007 by an engineer named Jeff Lindsay, borrowing the older programming idea of a "hook," a place where you arrange for something of yours to be called when an event fires. The picture to keep is simpler than the history: it is a doorbell the service rings, so you do not have to keep knocking.

### 8.2 Why the doorbell needs an address

There is a catch, and it is an honest and instructive one, because it is where this volume's territory reaches into the territory of Volume IV.

For the shop to _ring_ Mara, it needs somewhere to ring. When Mara does the knocking, she can knock from anywhere, from her laptop, which can be closed and reopened at will, because she is the one reaching out. But for the shop to reach _her_ , unprompted, at any hour, there has to be something of Mara's that is always awake and always listening at a fixed address on the internet, ready to receive the ring even at 3 a.m. when her laptop is shut and she is asleep.

A closed laptop cannot receive a doorbell. So a doorbell needs a _listener that is always on_ , sitting at a known address, which is precisely the thing Volume IV was about: a server, a small always-awake presence on the internet that you can point to. This is the honest bridge between the two volumes. The moment you want to be _rung_ rather than to _knock_ , you have stepped out of the world of "my laptop, when it's open" and into the world of "something of mine that never sleeps." You do not have to build that today, and you do not have to master it here; you only have to understand _why_ a doorbell implies one. The knocking approach needs no such thing, which is part of why knocking, for all its waste, is often the simpler place to start.


### 8.3 Polling or push: a judgment, not a doctrine

Here is where it becomes a decision rather than a rule. Knocking (the polite word is _polling_) and being-rung (the word is _push_) each have their place, and choosing well is a small act of judgment, not a matter of one being always right.

Being rung is wonderful when you truly need to know _right away_ and the delay of knocking would cost you something: a new order to pack, a payment that failed and needs handling, a message that needs a fast reply. It is worth the extra machinery of an always-on listener because immediacy has real value here.

Knocking is perfectly fine, and often better, when _right away_ does not actually matter. If Mara only assembles her orders once a week on Monday, she does not need a doorbell for them; she needs to knock once, on Monday, and read what came in. Building an always-on listener for a weekly task would be effort spent buying immediacy she has no use for. Much of the wisdom of automation is recognizing when you do _not_ need the fancier thing, and this is a clean example: a weekly digest wants a clock, not a doorbell.

So the question to ask of any "tell me when X happens" wish is: _do I need to know the instant it happens, or would knowing on a schedule be fine?_ If the instant matters, reach for the doorbell, and accept that it needs an always-on address. If a schedule is fine, knock on that schedule and keep your life simpler. Neither answer is more sophisticated than the other. The sophisticated thing is choosing the right one for the need.

#### Common Misconception

_"Webhooks are the advanced, correct way, and polling is the primitive thing beginners do."_

This is a status error, and it leads people to build complicated always-on listeners for tasks that a simple weekly knock would serve better. Polling and webhooks are not a ladder from worse to better; they are two tools for two different needs. Polling is genuinely the right choice whenever immediacy does not matter, and it has a real advantage: it needs nothing always-on, so it is simpler and has less to go wrong. Webhooks are the right choice when you truly need to know at once, and they carry a real cost: they require an always-listening address, which is more to set up and maintain. Choosing polling for a weekly task is not primitive; it is correct. Reaching for a webhook you do not need is not advanced; it is over-building. Match the tool to the need, and let go of the idea that fancier is better.


### 8.4 Mara's two rhythms

Mara's pipeline, by the end of this book, will actually use both, and seeing why makes the judgment concrete.

Her weekly assembly, reading the weekend's orders to update inventory and draft thank-you notes, does not need a doorbell. It happens on a rhythm she chose: Monday morning. For that, a knock on a schedule is exactly right, and Chapter 11 will show where such a scheduled knock lives.

But suppose one of her pieces is a commission, made to order, where a new order means she needs to start work _today_ and confirm the buyer's details while they are still at their keyboard. For _that_ , she wants the doorbell: the instant such an order lands, she wants to be rung, so nothing waits until Monday. That doorbell needs an always-on listener, a small presence on a server, and that is a fair price for immediacy that genuinely matters to her craft.

One person, two rhythms, chosen on purpose: a clock for the routine weekly work, a doorbell for the thing that cannot wait. That is what holding the map looks like in practice. You are not applying a rule. You are asking, each time, what the task actually needs, and reaching for the tool that fits.


### 8.5 Exercises

Read the answers.


#### Judgment scenario

**Q1.** For each wish, decide whether Mara should _knock on a schedule_ or _set up a doorbell_ , and say what each choice would require: (a) "Once a week, gather my orders and update my inventory sheet." (b) "The instant a rush commission comes in, alert me so I can start it today."

**Answer:** (a) is a clean case for _knocking on a schedule_ : "once a week" is a rhythm, immediacy does not matter, so the pipeline should knock every Monday and read what came in. This requires only something that runs on a clock (Chapter 11), no always-on listener. (b) is a clean case for a _doorbell_ : "the instant" means immediacy is the whole point, so Mara wants to be rung the moment the order lands. This requires an always-on listener at a fixed address, a small presence on a server (the Volume IV bridge), which is a fair cost for immediacy that genuinely matters. The lesson is that the wish's own words ("once a week" versus "the instant") tell you which tool fits.

#### Predict the service

**Q2.** Mara sets up a doorbell so her shop rings her whenever a new order arrives. She tests it by placing a fake order in the sandbox, and nothing rings, even though the order clearly appears in the shop. Before assuming the doorbell is broken, what is the most likely ordinary explanation, given section 8.2?

**Answer:** The most likely explanation is that there is nothing _listening_ at the address the doorbell rings, or the address is not reachable, because a doorbell needs an always-on listener at a fixed spot on the internet and a laptop or a not-yet-running listener will simply miss the ring. The shop may have rung faithfully; if no one was home to hear it, nothing happens. This is the practical face of section 8.2: the doorbell half is easy, but the _being reachable_ half depends on that always-on presence from Volume IV's world. Before suspecting the shop, check that your listener is actually up, always-on, and reachable at the address you gave. Many a "broken webhook" is just a doorbell ringing an empty house.


#### Say this to your AI

This chapter's ask teaches your assistant to make the polling-versus-push judgment _with_ you, rather than defaulting to the fancier option.

> _"When I want to be told that something happened, help me decide how. Ask me first: do I need to know the very instant it happens, or would finding out on a regular schedule be good enough? If a schedule is fine, set it up to check on that schedule and keep it simple. If I truly need to know at once, tell me plainly that this will need something of mine that's always on and listening, so I understand the cost before we build it. Don't reach for the always-on version unless the immediacy is really worth it."_

This ask puts the chapter's judgment where it belongs: in a short conversation before building, not in a reflex. It makes your assistant surface the real trade-off (immediacy versus the cost of an always-on listener), forbids the common over-build of a doorbell for a task a clock would serve, and keeps you the one deciding what your need actually is. It also quietly sets up Chapter 11, where the "something that runs on a schedule" and the "something always on" get proper homes.

### Chapter Summary

There are two ways to learn that something happened: **knocking** (your pipeline asks the counter every so often, a compromise between freshness and courtesy) and being **rung** (the service reaches out to you the moment the event happens). The second is a **webhook** , a doorbell: you register an address and a list of events, and the service rings you unprompted, often handing over a little box of JSON about what occurred. The name dates to 2007 and the engineer Jeff Lindsay, but the picture is all you need. The doorbell dissolves the freshness-versus-courtesy tension, at one honest cost: for a service to _ring_ you at any hour, you need something always awake and listening at a fixed address, which is precisely the always-on presence Volume IV was about. A closed laptop cannot receive a doorbell.

Choosing between knocking (**polling**) and being-rung (**push**) is a judgment, not a doctrine: reach for the doorbell only when you genuinely need to know _right away_ , and knock on a schedule when _right away_ does not matter, because a weekly task wants a clock, not an always-on listener, and over-building the fancier thing is a common error. Mara ends up using both: a scheduled knock for her weekly assembly, a doorbell for a rush commission that cannot wait. This built on Chapter 7's "ask once and remember" (the doorbell is the ultimate version of not-over-asking) and reached into Volume IV's territory. Next, Chapter 9 turns to a skill that makes every service approachable: reading its documentation the map way, scanning for what it _can do_ rather than memorizing how, and it is the pivot from the API map to the automation map.

* * *

---

blocks.en_title: Chapter 9: Reading the Map, Not the Manual
blocks.src:
Sooner or later you will want to do something with a service you have never touched. Mara, having tamed her orders, decides she wants her mailing list to do more: perhaps to tag buyers who bought a particular collection, so she can tell them first when she makes more. She has never looked under the hood of her mailing-list service. How does she find out whether it can even do this?

The answer is: she reads its documentation. And here is where most people flinch, because a service's documentation looks, at first glance, like exactly the wall this book promised you could ignore: pages of endpoints, tables of parameters, a reference so dense it seems written to exclude you. It genuinely was, once. But you are going to read it a completely different way than the people it was written for, and the difference is the whole chapter. They read it as a _manual_. You are going to read it as a _map_.


### 9.1 Two ways to read a set of docs

A programmer reads documentation to _memorize how_ : the exact name of each endpoint, the precise spelling of each parameter, the order the pieces go in. They need this because they are the ones typing the request, and the machine is unforgiving about spelling. That reading is slow, detailed, and exhausting, and it is not your reading.

You read documentation to _discover what_ : what can this service be asked to do, at all? Can the mailing list tag people? Can it tell me who opened a message? Can it be asked to add someone to a group? You are not trying to learn the spelling of anything. You are taking inventory of the service's _powers_ , the way you would skim a restaurant's menu to see whether they serve breakfast, without memorizing a single recipe. This reading is fast, high-level, and genuinely pleasant once you give yourself permission to skip the parts written for the person who does the typing.


#### Definition: Capability scanning

**Capability scanning** is reading a service's documentation to answer one question, _what can this thing be asked to do for someone like me?_ , while deliberately ignoring the exact syntax of how. You are surveying the service's powers, not memorizing its commands. It is the map-reader's way through documentation, and it is fast precisely because it skips everything the manual-reader has to slog through.

Almost every service's docs are organized, whether they say so or not, into two layers. There is an _overview_ or _guide_ layer, written in something close to plain language, that describes what the service is for and the broad shapes of things it can do. And there is a _reference_ layer, the dense tables, that spells out every detail of every request. The map-reader lives in the first layer and visits the second only at the last minute, at _commissioning time_ , when an automation is actually being built and your assistant needs the exact spelling. Until then, the reference is not your concern. Find the guide. Read the powers. Close the tab.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 9: Reading the Map, Not the Manual
blocks.src:
### 9.2 Let your assistant do the slog

Here is the part that should feel like a relief: even the capability scan is mostly your assistant's job, and your job is to read its report and ask the right follow-up.

You do not have to open a service's docs yourself and hunt for the capabilities page. You can hand the whole reading to your assistant and ask it to come back with the map: "read this service's documentation and tell me, in plain words, what it can and can't do for someone like me." Your assistant is a fast, tireless reader of dense reference material, and turning that material into a plain-language inventory of powers is exactly the kind of thing it is good at. What comes back is a survey you can actually use to decide what is possible, without your ever touching the reference tables.

But, and this is the supervision the whole book keeps insisting on, you read that survey critically. A service's _real_ documented powers are a fact you can check. If your assistant claims the mailing list can do something, that claim should trace back to the service's actual docs, not to the assistant's confident guess. So the good follow-up is: "and where in the docs does it say it can do that?" This matters more here than almost anywhere, because a plausible-sounding but invented capability is exactly the kind of thing that leads you to commission an automation the service cannot actually perform. Trust the assistant to _read fast_ ; verify that what it reports is really in the text.


### 9.3 The best gift in the docs: the sandbox

When you scan a new service's docs, there is one capability worth hunting for specifically, because it changes how safely you can explore everything else: a **sandbox** , sometimes called test mode.

A sandbox is a complete pretend version of the service, where nothing is real. Orders placed there are fake. Emails "sent" there go nowhere. Money "charged" there is imaginary. It exists precisely so that people can try things, make mistakes, and learn a service's behavior without any real-world consequence. Paired with the _test keys_ from Chapter 6, a sandbox lets you and your assistant wire up a whole automation, run it, watch it misbehave, fix it, and run it again, all without a single real customer being emailed or a single real dollar moving.

This is the docs' best gift, and a great many services offer it, so it is worth asking about every time. When Mara wants to experiment with tagging her buyers, the responsible first move is not to try it on her real mailing list with her real customers. It is to ask whether the service has a sandbox, and to do all her learning there. A service that offers a sandbox is telling you, in effect, "here is a safe place to be wrong." Take it up on the offer. Being wrong safely, many times, is how you come to trust a pipe before you point it at anything real.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 9: Reading the Map, Not the Manual
blocks.src:
#### Common Misconception

_"I need to understand a service's documentation thoroughly before I can use it."_

You need to understand its _capabilities_ , which is the fast, top-layer reading, not its _reference_ , which is the slow, detailed one. People imagine they must read the whole dense manual cover to cover before they are "allowed" to do anything, and that belief is what makes them give up before they start, because the reference layer is genuinely exhausting and mostly irrelevant to a person who is not doing the typing. The truth is the reverse: you do a fast scan of what the service _can do_ , decide what you want, and only _then_ , at commissioning time, does anyone (your assistant, usually) need the exact reference details for the one specific thing you chose. You do not eat the whole menu to order breakfast. Read for powers, choose, and let the details arrive just in time.


### 9.4 The pivot: from what services are to what to do with them

Notice that this chapter sits on a hinge. The first eight chapters were about what services _are_ and how they behave: counter windows, JSON, asks and answers, refusals, keys, courtesy, doorbells. You now hold that map. Capability scanning is the skill that lets you point that map at _any_ service, including ones neither of us has heard of, and quickly learn its shape.

That completes the API half of the book. From here, the question changes. It is no longer "what is this service and how does it behave?" It is "given that I can now find out what any service can do, _which of these powers are worth wiring together, and which should I leave alone?_ " That is the automation half of the book, and it is where judgment moves from the background to the foreground. Capability scanning is the bridge: it is the last skill of the "understanding services" half and the first tool of the "commissioning automations" half, because you cannot decide what is worth automating until you can quickly survey what is possible.

So the ask that closes this chapter is, fittingly, the ask that opens every automation you will ever build: before deciding what to do, find out what can be done.


### 9.5 Exercises

Read the answers.


#### Say this to your AI (rehearsal)

**Q1.** Mara wants to know whether her mailing-list service can tag buyers by which collection they bought, so she can message those groups later. Write, in your own words, the plain-language ask she should make to her assistant, and name the one follow-up question she must not skip.

Hint

She wants a survey of powers, in plain words, and she wants to be able to trust it.

**Answer:** A good ask is something like: "Read my mailing-list service's documentation and tell me, in plain words, whether it can tag or group buyers by which collection they bought, and what else it can do along those lines. Don't set anything up; I just want to know what's possible." The follow-up she must not skip is: "and where in the docs does it actually say that?" That second question is the whole difference between capability scanning and wishful thinking, because it forces the assistant's report back onto the service's real, checkable text rather than a plausible guess. Reading fast is the assistant's gift; verifying that what it read is really there is Mara's job, and it is a small job with a large payoff.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 9: Reading the Map, Not the Manual
blocks.src:
#### Judgment scenario

**Q2.** Your assistant scans a new payments service's docs and reports back: "Good news, it can issue refunds automatically, and I found a sandbox where we can test everything with fake money." You are excited to build a refund automation. What should you do _first_ , before wiring anything to your real account, and why does the sandbox make this the obvious move?

**Answer:** First, build and run the whole thing _in the sandbox_ , with test keys, using fake money, and watch it behave across several trial refunds before it ever touches a real account. The sandbox makes this obvious because it removes the entire cost of being wrong: a mistaken or runaway refund automation aimed at real money is exactly the kind of high-blast-radius disaster Chapter 6's 3 a.m. question warns about, but the same mistake in the sandbox costs nothing and teaches you everything. Refunds move money, which is the careful territory, so the sandbox is not an optional nicety here; it is the responsible path. You earn trust in a money-touching pipe by watching it behave harmlessly, many times, before you let it near the real thing. Chapter 12 will make this posture a formal habit.


#### Say this to your AI

This chapter's standing ask makes capability scanning your assistant's default first move with any unfamiliar service.

> _"Whenever I'm curious whether some service can do a thing for me, start by reading its documentation and giving me a plain-words summary of what it can and can't do for someone like me, and point to where in the docs each capability is actually described, so I can trust it. Always check whether it offers a sandbox or test mode, and tell me if it does. Don't build anything yet; I want the survey first, and then we'll decide together what's worth doing."_

This ask installs the whole chapter as a habit: capability scanning first (powers, in plain words), verification second (point to the docs), sandbox-hunting always (a safe place to be wrong), and building never-before-deciding. It turns your assistant into a fast scout who brings back a trustworthy map of any service's territory, and it keeps the decision about what to _do_ with that territory firmly with you. It is, not by accident, the ask that every automation in the rest of the book begins with.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 9: Reading the Map, Not the Manual
blocks.src:
### Chapter Summary

Documentation looks like a wall because it was written for the person doing the typing, who reads it as a **manual** to memorize _how_. You read it as a **map** , doing **capability scanning** : skimming for _what this service can be asked to do for someone like me_ , while ignoring the exact syntax until commissioning time. Almost every service's docs split into a plain-language guide layer (where the map-reader lives) and a dense reference layer (visited only at the last minute), so you find the guide, read the powers, and close the tab. Better still, this scan is mostly your assistant's job: have it read the dense material and report the powers in plain words, then supervise by asking _where in the docs it says so_ , because a plausible invented capability is exactly what leads to commissioning something a service cannot do. And always hunt for the docs' best gift, a **sandbox** : a pretend version of the service where, paired with test keys, you can be wrong safely as many times as it takes to earn trust in a pipe.

This chapter is the hinge of the book. It completes the API half (it is the skill that points your map at _any_ service) and opens the automation half (you cannot decide what is worth automating until you can survey what is possible). It built on Chapter 6's test keys and the whole book's habit of supervising rather than trusting blindly. Next, Chapter 10 asks the first real question of the automation half, and it is a question of judgment, not machinery: of everything a service _can_ do, _what actually deserves to be automated_ , and what is better left in your own hands?

* * *

---

Now that you can survey what any service is able to do, a seductive danger appears: the temptation to automate everything, just because you can.

Resist it. The most valuable skill on the automation map is not building pipes. It is judging _which_ pipes are worth building, because every automation is a small standing commitment, a thing that will run without you and, someday, break without you. An automation you should not have built is worse than the manual task it replaced, because now you have both the work _and_ a fragile machine to maintain. So before we talk about how automations run, we talk about which ones deserve to exist. This is a chapter of judgment, and judgment is the human's permanent job.


### 10.1 The three things worth automating

Look back at Mara's Monday and ask what makes those tasks good candidates. Three qualities recur, and they are the honest test for anything you consider handing off.

**The recurring.** A task you do again and again, on a rhythm, is worth automating precisely because the effort of building the pipe is paid back every time it runs. Mara's order-reading happens every single week, forever. Building it once to run a hundred times is a good trade. A task you will do exactly once is almost never worth automating; you would spend longer building the pipe than doing the thing.

**The error-prone.** A task where a human hand slips, where you transpose a number, skip a row, paste into the wrong cell, is worth handing to a machine that does not get tired or distracted. Mara copying order details into a spreadsheet by hand is exactly this: dull, repetitive, and quietly error-prone at row forty. A machine copies row forty as carefully as row one.

**The boring.** A task that requires no judgment, no creativity, nothing that is distinctly yours, is a task you are wasting yourself on. The copying and pasting is boring. The paragraph about the new kiln pieces is not; it is Mara's voice, her craft, the part her buyers actually want from her. Automate the boring so you have more of yourself left for the parts that are not.

Notice that Mara's Monday tasks are strong on all three: recurring, error-prone, boring. That is why they were such good candidates that we opened the whole book with them. The stronger a task is on these three, the more clearly it deserves a pipe.

### 10.2 The things to leave alone

Just as important, and more often ignored, is knowing what _not_ to automate. Three qualities mark a task as better left in human hands.

**The rare.** If you do it once a year, or once ever, building an automation for it is effort you will never earn back, and you will have a fragile pipe sitting unused, quietly rotting, until the one day you need it and discover it broke months ago. Do the rare thing by hand.

**The judgment-laden.** If doing the task _well_ requires taste, discretion, care, or a human reading of a situation, then automating it does not save you the hard part; it removes the hard part badly. Mara could technically automate the writing of her weekly newsletter paragraph, but the paragraph is the point; a machine-written version would be worse in exactly the way that matters. The judgment-laden task is where _you_ add the value. Keep it.

**The two-minute task.** If a thing genuinely takes two minutes and you do it occasionally, the honest accounting often says: just do it. Building, testing, and maintaining an automation for a two-minute occasional task can cost more, in total, than years of just doing it. There is no shame in a manual step. Sometimes it is simply the right answer, and a mature map-reader knows this and is not embarrassed by it.


#### Common Misconception

_"If a task can be automated, it should be."_

This is the error that turns a capable person into the exhausted keeper of a dozen brittle pipes. _Can_ and _should_ are different questions, and the gap between them is judgment. Every automation you build is a permanent tenant: it takes up space, it needs occasional maintenance, and it will eventually break at an inconvenient time and demand your attention. That rent is worth paying for a task that is recurring, error-prone, and boring, because the pipe saves you real and repeated effort. It is a bad trade for a task that is rare, judgment-laden, or trivially quick, because you pay the rent forever to avoid work that was small, or that only you could do well anyway. The mark of skill is not how much you automate. It is how well you choose. Automate the boring and the repeated; keep the rare, the delicate, and the tiny.


### 10.3 The universal shape: WHEN this, THEN that

Once you have decided a task is worth automating, almost every automation you will ever describe takes the same, wonderfully simple shape. Learn it and you can describe any pipe you can imagine.

#### Definition: The WHEN-THEN pipeline

An automation is a piece of **WHEN-this-THEN-that** plumbing: _when_ some trigger happens, _then_ some action follows. The trigger is what sets it off (a schedule arrives, a doorbell rings, a condition becomes true). The action is what it does in response (read something, write something somewhere, send a message). Longer pipes are just chains of these: when this, then that, and then that, and then this other thing. Every automation, however grand, is built from this one modest sentence.

Watch how Mara's whole Monday collapses into it. _When_ Monday morning arrives (the trigger, a schedule), _then_ read the weekend's new orders, _and then_ update the inventory sheet, _and then_ draft a thank-you note for each paid buyer. One trigger, a chain of actions. Her rush-commission alert is another: _when_ a commission order arrives (the trigger, a doorbell), _then_ alert Mara at once. The triggers differ (a clock versus a doorbell, exactly the Chapter 8 choice), but the shape is identical.

This shape is a gift, because it means you never have to imagine complex machinery to commission an automation. You only have to finish two sentences: "when does this run?" and "what does it do when it runs?" If you can answer those in plain words, you can commission the pipe, and your assistant can build it. The plumbing is real, but its blueprint is a single sentence you already know how to speak.


### 10.4 Small before grand

There is one more piece of judgment, and it is the one that keeps automation from turning into heartbreak: start small, and watch.

The temptation, once you can build pipes, is to design a magnificent one: a great interconnected system that handles your entire Monday, all four tasks, in one grand automated flow, switched on all at once. Do not. Build the smallest useful pipe first, the single most boring task, and then _watch it for a week_. Watch what it does. Watch how it fails. Watch the ways the real world surprises it, the order with a missing field, the buyer with an odd name, the week the service is slow. Only when that one small pipe has earned your trust do you add the next.

The reason is not timidity. It is that automations meet the real world, and the real world is messy in ways no plan anticipates, and a small pipe teaches you those ways cheaply while a grand pipe hides them until they fail all at once and you cannot tell which part broke. A pipe you watched for a week is a pipe you understand. A grand system switched on all at once is a mystery you have to debug under pressure. This is also the beginning of the answer to a fear you may be carrying, _I couldn't maintain it_ : you maintain a big automation by having built it as a series of small, understood ones, each of which you watched until you trusted it. Nobody maintains a mystery. Everybody can maintain a thing they watched grow.


### 10.5 Exercises

Read the answers.

#### Judgment scenario

**Q1.** For each task, decide whether Mara should automate it or keep it by hand, and name which qualities from this chapter drive your answer: (a) copying each week's paid orders into her inventory sheet; (b) writing the warm paragraph about her new kiln pieces; (c) filing her annual business taxes; (d) sending each paid buyer a thank-you-and-shipping note.

**Answer:** (a) _Automate_ : it is recurring (weekly), error-prone (hand-copying rows), and boring (no judgment), strong on all three, an ideal candidate. (b) _Keep by hand_ : it is judgment-laden and creative; the paragraph is Mara's voice and craft, exactly the part that must not be automated away. (c) _Keep by hand_ (or use a human professional): it is rare (once a year) and judgment-laden, so building a pipe would be effort never earned back for a task that needs human care anyway. (d) _Automate, but carefully_ : it is recurring and boring, so it deserves a pipe, but it _sends_ something into the world to a real customer, and that (not any error-proneness) is what puts it in the careful territory (draft-don't-send, per Chapter 12). The pattern: automate the recurring-boring-repetitive, keep the rare-and-delicate, and flag anything that _sends_ for extra care.


#### Predict the shape

**Q2.** Rewrite this wish as a WHEN-THEN pipeline, naming the trigger and the chain of actions: "Every Monday, I want my orders gathered, my inventory updated, and a thank-you drafted for each paid buyer."

**Answer:** _Trigger (WHEN):_ Monday morning arrives, a schedule. _Actions (THEN, in a chain):_ read the weekend's new orders; then update the inventory sheet from those orders; then, for each order whose `paid` box is true, draft a thank-you-and-shipping note. In one sentence: _when Monday comes, then read the orders, and then update inventory, and then draft the paid-buyers' thank-yous._ Notice three things this exercise reveals: the trigger is a clock (so this wants a scheduled knock, not a doorbell); the chain reuses the labeled-box reading from Chapter 3 (the `paid` fact is one such box, read to decide who gets a note); and the final action is _draft_ , not _send_ , keeping a human hand on the part that goes out into the world. The whole of Mara's Monday, and it fit in one WHEN-THEN sentence.

#### Say this to your AI

This chapter's ask makes your assistant a partner in _judgment_ , not just a builder, so it helps you choose well before it helps you build.

> _"When I bring you an idea for automating something, don't just build it. First help me judge whether it's worth it: is this task recurring, error-prone, and boring enough to deserve a pipe, or is it rare, judgment-heavy, or so quick I should just keep doing it by hand? If it's worth automating, help me describe it as a simple 'when this happens, then do that' plan, and let's start with the smallest useful version and watch it for a week before we add anything. And always flag for me if any step actually sends something out into the world, so we can be extra careful with those."_

This ask installs the whole chapter as a working habit: the can-versus-should judgment (the three qualities each way), the WHEN-THEN blueprint, the small-before-grand discipline of watching one pipe for a week, and a standing flag on any _sending_ step. It turns your assistant from an eager builder into a thoughtful collaborator who helps you avoid the fate that misconception leads to. Choosing well is the skill; this ask keeps the choosing in the conversation.


### Chapter Summary

The most valuable skill of the automation half is not building pipes but judging which deserve to exist, because every automation is a permanent tenant that runs without you and eventually breaks without you. Automate the **recurring** , the **error-prone** , and the **boring** , where the pipe pays back its cost every run and frees you for the parts that are actually yours. Leave alone the **rare** (never earns its cost back), the **judgment-laden** (where you add the value), and the **two-minute task** (where doing it by hand is simply cheaper), because _can_ and _should_ are different questions and the gap between them is judgment. Once a task passes the test, almost every automation takes one shape: **WHEN this, THEN that** , a trigger followed by a chain of actions, so commissioning a pipe is just finishing two sentences, "when does it run?" and "what does it do?" And you build safely by going **small before grand** : the smallest useful pipe first, watched for a week until it earns trust, because you maintain big automations by having grown them from small, understood ones.

This chapter began to answer the fear _I couldn't maintain it_ : nobody maintains a mystery, but anyone can maintain a thing they watched grow. It built on Chapter 9's capability scanning (you judge what to automate only after surveying what is possible), Chapter 8's clock-versus-doorbell triggers, and Chapter 3's labeled-box filtering (the `paid` fact as a safety check). Next, Chapter 11 answers the practical question the WHEN-THEN shape raises: once you have described a pipe, _where does it actually live and run_ , on your machine, on a schedule, or on something always on?

* * *

---

You have described a pipe: when this, then that. But a description is not a running thing. A WHEN-THEN plan has to _live_ somewhere, on some actual machine that is awake when the trigger fires and does the actions. So the practical question this chapter answers is deceptively simple and genuinely important: where does your automation run?

There are three homes, and choosing among them is not about which is best. It is about what your particular pipe needs. A pipe that runs when you say so needs one home. A pipe that runs on a schedule needs another. A pipe that must be reachable at any hour needs a third. Match the home to the need, and the choice makes itself. The whole chapter is learning to feel that match.


### 11.1 The first home: your own machine, when you're there

The simplest home for an automation is the machine in front of you, right now, run when you ask.

You say to your assistant, "gather this week's orders and draft the thank-yous," and it runs the pipe then and there, on your laptop, while you watch. This is the natural home for anything you _initiate_ , anything where you are present and want to be. It needs nothing special. It is where every automation should probably begin its life, because running a pipe while you watch is exactly the "small before grand, watch it for a week" discipline from Chapter 10, made literal.

But this home has one hard limit, and it defines everything else: **your machine is not always on.** When you close the laptop, the pipe stops existing. It cannot run at midnight if the lid is shut. It cannot receive a doorbell while you sleep. So the first home is perfect for "run this now, while I'm here" and useless for "run this every night" or "be ready whenever an order lands." The moment a pipe needs to act when you are _not_ there, it has to move out.

### 11.2 The second home: your machine, on a schedule

The next step up answers "run this every night" without asking you to be awake for it. You arrange for the pipe to run _on a schedule_ , at times you set in advance, so it fires whether or not you are paying attention, as long as the machine is on.

There is a decades-old tool for exactly this, and you met its world in Volume III: a scheduler, a kind of tireless calendar-clerk that sits quietly and, at the appointed time, sets a task running. You tell it "every Monday at 8 a.m., run this pipe," and it does, faithfully, without being reminded. You do not have to know how to operate the clerk by hand; your assistant can set the schedule for you. What you need is the _concept_ : there is a way to have your machine run a pipe on a clock, unattended, and it is the right home for the recurring, scheduled tasks that make up so much of automation.

This home fits Mara's weekly assembly perfectly. Reading the weekend's orders is a "when Monday comes" task, a schedule, not a doorbell. If Mara's machine is on Monday morning (or if this scheduled pipe lives on something that is always on, which is the third home), the calendar-clerk fires it, the orders get read, the thank-yous get drafted, and Mara comes to a finished result rather than a chore. The scheduled home is where the clock-triggered half of Chapter 8 comes to rest.

There is a catch worth naming honestly: a schedule on _your_ machine only fires if your machine happens to be on and awake at that time. If your laptop is asleep at 8 a.m. Monday, the clerk cannot fire the task. For a weekly task that is often fine, you just run it when you next open the lid. But for anything that truly must happen on time regardless of you, the schedule itself needs a home that never sleeps, which brings us to the third.


### 11.3 The third home: something always on

Some pipes cannot live on a machine that sleeps. A doorbell, from Chapter 8, needs something awake and listening at a fixed address at every hour, because an order can land at 3 a.m. and the ring has to be received. A schedule that absolutely must fire on time, every time, needs the same. For these, the home is a small, always-on presence on the internet, which is exactly what Volume IV was about: a server, a machine that is not yours-in-front-of-you but yours-out-there, awake around the clock, reachable at a known address.

You do not have to build or master this to understand the map. What matters is recognizing _when a pipe needs it_. The test is simple: does this pipe have to act when I am definitely not there and my own machine is definitely off? If yes, it needs the always-on home. A doorbell needs it. A digest that must go out at exactly 6 a.m. whether or not you are awake needs it. A "run this whenever I ask" pipe does not, and a "run this weekly, whenever my machine is next on" pipe often does not either. The always-on home is more to set up and maintain, so you reach for it only when the pipe genuinely cannot live anywhere simpler.

A small pin for readers of Volume II: privacy can also decide _where_ a piece of a pipe lives. The worker that drafts from sensitive material can be a _local model_ , your own private AI on your own always-on machine, keeping that work in-house, which is Volume II's world. The capstone returns to this.

#### Common Misconception

_"Real automations run 'in the cloud'; running things on my own laptop is just playing around."_

This mixes up sophistication with suitability. Running a pipe on your own machine, while you watch, is not a toy stage you graduate out of; it is the correct and responsible home for a large class of automations, especially while you are learning one and watching it for a week. Plenty of genuinely useful pipes never need to leave your machine, because they run when you ask and you are there when they run. The always-on home is not a badge of seriousness; it is a specific answer to a specific need, "this must act when I'm not here," and it carries real extra cost in setup and upkeep. Choosing your own machine when that is all a pipe needs is not playing around. It is matching the home to the need, which is the actual skill.


### 11.4 Mara's two homes

Mara's finished setup uses two of the three homes, and seeing which goes where makes the whole choice concrete.

Her **weekly assembly** , the order-reading, inventory-updating, thank-you-drafting pipe, is scheduled. It does not need to fire at a precise second, and it does not need to receive anything unprompted; it just needs to run each week. So it lives as a scheduled task, and whether that schedule sits on her own machine (firing when she opens the lid Monday) or on a small always-on machine (firing at 8 a.m. sharp regardless) is a choice she makes based on how much the exact timing matters to her. For a weekly draft she will review anyway, her own machine is honestly fine.

Her **rush-commission doorbell** , the one that must catch an order the instant it lands so she can start the piece today, cannot live on a sleeping laptop. It needs the always-on home: a small presence out there, awake at every hour, listening at a fixed address for the shop to ring. This is the one piece of Mara's automation that genuinely reaches into Volume IV's world, and it does so for a clear reason she can name: immediacy that her craft actually needs.

One person, three homes available, two of them used, each chosen by asking what the pipe needs rather than which is fanciest. That is the chapter, and it is the whole discipline: the home is not a status symbol; it is a fit.


### 11.5 Exercises

Read the answers.

#### Judgment scenario

**Q1.** For each pipe, name the home it should live in (your machine when you're there; your machine on a schedule; something always on) and why: (a) "Whenever I ask, summarize my new emails." (b) "Every Monday, gather my orders and draft thank-yous; I'll review them when I sit down." (c) "The instant a payment fails, alert me so I can fix it before the customer notices."

**Answer:** (a) _Your machine, when you're there_ : you initiate it, you are present, it needs nothing always-on. This is the simplest home and exactly right for on-demand tasks. (b) _Your machine on a schedule_ is fine: it is a weekly, clock-triggered task you will review anyway, so it does not need precise timing or an always-on presence; the calendar-clerk fires it when your machine is on Monday. (If Mara wanted it done at 8 a.m. sharp regardless of her laptop, she would move just this schedule to an always-on home.) (c) _Something always on_ : "the instant a payment fails" is a doorbell needing immediacy at any hour, so it must be received by something awake and listening around the clock. The pattern: on-demand stays local, scheduled-and-flexible stays local or scheduled, and instant-at-any-hour needs the always-on home.


#### Predict the need

**Q2.** A friend says, "I've built an automation on my laptop that's supposed to email me a summary every morning at 6 a.m., but half the time it doesn't arrive." Given this chapter, what is the most likely ordinary cause, and what is the fix?

**Answer:** The most likely cause is that the friend's laptop is _asleep or off_ at 6 a.m. on the mornings the summary fails to arrive, so the calendar-clerk cannot fire the task; a schedule on your own machine only runs if the machine is awake at that time. The fix is to move this particular scheduled pipe to an always-on home, a small machine that never sleeps, so 6 a.m. always finds something awake to run it. This is the sleeping-laptop catch, met in the flesh: scheduling is only as reliable as the machine's wakefulness, and a task that must happen _on time regardless of you_ has outgrown the sleeping-laptop home. Note that the pipe itself is fine; only its home was wrong for the need.


#### Say this to your AI

This chapter's ask makes your assistant reason about _where_ a pipe lives as a deliberate choice tied to need, and flag when a pipe has outgrown a simpler home.

> _"Whenever we set up an automation, help me decide where it should run. If it's something I kick off while I'm here, let's just run it on my own machine. If it needs to happen on a schedule, tell me plainly that it'll only fire when my machine is actually on, and ask me whether the exact timing matters enough to need something that's always on. And if it needs to react the instant something happens, or run at a precise time no matter what, tell me clearly that this one needs an always-on home, and why, before we build it, so I'm choosing that cost on purpose."_

This ask installs the three-homes judgment as a habit: local for on-demand, scheduled with its honest catch spelled out, and always-on reserved for genuine immediacy or must-fire timing, chosen deliberately because of its extra cost. It keeps you from both mistakes at once, running an always-on task on a sleeping laptop, and over-building an always-on home for a task your own machine would serve. The home is a fit, and this ask makes your assistant help you find it.

### Chapter Summary

A WHEN-THEN plan has to _live_ on an actual machine that is awake when the trigger fires, and there are three homes, chosen by need rather than status. The first is **your own machine, when you're there** : perfect for on-demand pipes you initiate and watch, and the right place for every automation to begin its life, but useless the moment a pipe must act while you are away, because your machine is not always on. The second is **your machine on a schedule** , run by a tireless calendar-clerk (the scheduler from Volume III's world) that fires a pipe on a clock unattended, with one honest catch: it only fires if the machine is actually awake at that time. The third is **something always on** , a small presence out on the internet (Volume IV's server) that is awake at every hour and reachable at a fixed address, which is what a doorbell needs, and what a must-fire-on-time schedule needs, at the cost of more setup and upkeep.

The discipline is to match the home to the need: on-demand stays local, scheduled-and-flexible stays local or scheduled, and instant-at-any-hour earns the always-on home. Mara uses two homes, a scheduled weekly assembly and an always-on rush-commission doorbell, each chosen by asking what the pipe requires. We also pinned Volume II here: an always-on home can host a private local model as a pipe's worker when privacy should shape where the work happens. This built on Chapter 8's clock-versus-doorbell triggers and Chapter 10's small-before-grand discipline. Next, Chapter 12 crosses into the book's second heavyweight territory: the moment you let your assistant not just describe and build a pipe but _act_ through it, holding your keys, changing the world on your behalf, which is exactly why Chapter 6 mattered, squared.

* * *

---

blocks.en_title: Chapter 12: Handing the Agent the Keys
blocks.src:
Until now, your assistant has mostly been a reader and a builder. It reads services, drafts pipes, shows you answers. You have kept your hand on every action that touches the world. This chapter is about the moment you loosen that hand: when you let your assistant not just _describe_ an automation but _run_ it, holding your keys, acting on services on your behalf, changing things while you are not watching.

This is the second heavyweight chapter of the book, and it earns the weight, because this is where the stakes from Chapter 6 come fully due. A key was your identity in machine form. Now something is holding that identity and _acting_ with it, possibly at 3 a.m., possibly faster than you could ever stop it. That is not a reason to refuse. It is the whole promise of the book, the boring work finally doing itself. It is a reason to build a specific, calm set of habits so that when you hand over the keys, you hand them over _bounded_. This chapter is those habits. None of them is complicated. Together they are the difference between an automation that serves you and one that surprises you.


### 12.1 Blast radius: the question before every go-live

Before you let a pipe act on its own, you ask one honest question, the one introduced with the key in Chapter 6, now given its full ceremony:

_What is the worst this pipeline can do if it misfires at 3 a.m., while I am asleep and cannot stop it?_

We call the answer the pipe's **blast radius** : the full extent of what it could affect if it went wrong at the worst possible moment. The 3 a.m. framing is not drama; it is the honest test condition, because an automation runs unattended and if it fails it may well fail when no one is watching. So you imagine that moment and you answer plainly.

A pipe that only _reads_ has a tiny blast radius. Misfiring at 3 a.m., the worst it does is read Mara's orders a few extra times, which harms nothing. You can let a reading pipe run with a light hand. A pipe that _sends emails_ has a much larger radius: misfiring, it could email hundreds of real customers something wrong, and that cannot be un-sent. A pipe that _spends money_ has a larger radius still: misfiring, it could run up charges with no natural limit, because a machine does not get tired of spending. A pipe that _deletes_ things has among the largest: misfiring, it could destroy records that do not come back.

The blast radius is not a reason to avoid these pipes. It is a _map of where to put your guardrails_. A large radius does not mean "don't build it." It means "build it with test mode, spending caps, draft-don't-send, and a human hand on the trigger," each of which we take in turn. You answer the 3 a.m. question first precisely so that the guardrails you add are the ones that actually match the danger, rather than a vague, anxious over-caution sprayed everywhere.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 12: Handing the Agent the Keys
blocks.src:
### 12.2 Reversible or not: the deepest cut

Underneath blast radius sits one distinction that decides more than any other: is the action _reversible_?

Reading is perfectly reversible; it changes nothing. Some changes are easily undone: add the wrong tag to a customer, remove the tag. But some actions cannot be taken back at all. An email, once sent, is in someone's inbox forever. A public post, once posted, was seen. A payment, once made, has moved real money. A hard deletion, once done, may be gone.

Sort every action a pipe can take into these two bins, because they deserve opposite postures. Reversible actions you can let an assistant do more freely, because a mistake is a cleanup, not a catastrophe. Irreversible actions, the ones that _send_ , _post_ , _pay_ , or _destroy_ , deserve a human "yes" before they happen, at least until the pipe has earned deep trust, because a mistake there is permanent. This is the Chapter 1 reading-versus-sending line, followed all the way down to its most serious form. The single most protective instinct in all of automation is this: _let the machine do the reversible things; keep a hand on the irreversible ones._

blocks.en_title: Chapter 12: Handing the Agent the Keys
blocks.src:
### 12.3 The four calm guardrails

Here are the specific habits that bound a pipe's blast radius. They are calm and concrete, and together they let you hand over the keys without holding your breath.

**Test mode first.** Before a pipe touches anything real, run it in the sandbox from Chapter 9 (the service's own fake environment), entered with the test keys from Chapter 6 (a test identity, not your live one). The two work together: the sandbox is the _place_ where nothing is real, and the test key is _who you are_ while you are in it. Let it send fake emails and spend fake money and watch it behave across many runs. A pipe that has misbehaved a dozen times harmlessly in the sandbox is a pipe you understand before it ever meets a real customer. You do not earn trust in a money-touching pipe by arguing about it; you earn it by watching it be harmless, repeatedly, where being wrong costs nothing.

**Dry runs: "show me what you _would_ have done."** Even with a real pipe, you can ask it to go through all its motions and, at the final irreversible step, _stop and show you_ what it was about to do rather than doing it. Show me the emails you would have sent. Show me the charges you would have made. A dry run lets you inspect the pipe's intended action, in full, before a single irreversible thing happens. It is the single most useful posture for a nervous first real run.

**Spending caps.** For anything that can cost money, set a hard ceiling, at the service, that the pipe cannot exceed no matter what. A cap is a wall that does not depend on the pipe behaving. Even if the automation loses its mind at 3 a.m., the cap stops the bleeding at a number you chose while calm. Many services let you set exactly this, and for any money-touching pipe it is not optional; it is the floor of responsibility.

**Draft, don't send.** For messages that go out to real people, make the pipe's default _draft_ rather than _send_. Let it do all the tedious work, gathering the orders, writing each thank-you in your voice, assembling everything, and then leave the finished drafts for you to glance at and release. You keep the two seconds of human judgment that catch the wrong name, the half-written line, the note going to the buyer who has not actually paid. You lose almost none of the time saved, because the machine still did the drudgery. Draft-don't-send is how you automate a _sending_ task while keeping a hand on the _send_.


#### Definition: The safe-posture set

The **safe-posture set** is the standing collection of guardrails you apply when an automation acts on the world: answer the **3 a.m. question** to map the blast radius; sort actions into **reversible** (freer) and **irreversible** (human "yes"); run in **test mode first** ; use **dry runs** to preview irreversible steps; set **spending caps** on anything that costs; and default to **draft, don't send** for messages to real people. You do not apply all of them to every pipe; you apply the ones the blast radius calls for. A reading pipe needs almost none. A money-and-email pipe needs them all.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 12: Handing the Agent the Keys
blocks.src:
### 12.4 Reading the pipeline's diary

One more habit closes the loop, and it is the one that lets you sleep: a pipe that acts on its own should keep a **diary** , a running record of what it actually did each time it ran, so you can look back and check.

This diary (you may hear it called a log) is the gist-level idea that an automation writes down its own actions: on Monday at 8 a.m. it read fourteen orders, updated the sheet, drafted twelve thank-yous, skipped two unpaid. You do not have to watch a pipe run to trust it, if you can _read afterward_ what it did. The diary is how a pipe that acts while you sleep stays accountable to you: you wake up, you glance at the diary, you see it did exactly what it should have, and you carry on. And when something _does_ go wrong, the diary is where you find out what, because it recorded the action that misfired.

So when you commission an acting pipe, ask that it keep a plain, readable record of what it does, and get in the habit of glancing at it. A pipe you can read the diary of is a pipe you can trust to run unattended, because trust here does not mean "never checking"; it means "able to check." This is the same instinct as reading JSON from Chapter 3, extended across time: not faith that the pipe behaved, but the ability to see that it did.


#### Common Misconception

_"Letting an assistant act on its own means giving up control."_

It is the opposite, if you do it with the safe-posture set. Giving up control would be handing a pipe your master key, letting it send freely to real people with no cap and no draft step and no diary, and hoping. That is not what this chapter describes. What this chapter describes is handing over _bounded_ power: a narrowly scoped key, a spending cap the pipe cannot exceed, irreversible steps that draft rather than send or that pause for your "yes," a sandbox where it proved itself first, and a diary you can read after. That is not less control than doing the task by hand; in some ways it is _more_ , because the guardrails are explicit and enforced by the services themselves, rather than depending on your own tired attention at row forty. You did not give up the wheel. You gave the pipe brakes, a speed limiter, and a dashcam of your own making, the scoped key, the spending cap, the readable diary, and then you let it drive.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 12: Handing the Agent the Keys
blocks.src:
### 12.5 Mara hands over the thank-yous

Watch Mara cross this line, because she does it exactly right, and her caution is a model rather than a fear.

She wants her assistant to handle the weekly thank-you notes, a _sending_ task, to real customers, irreversible. So she runs the 3 a.m. question: worst case, a misfire emails the wrong things to real buyers, which cannot be un-sent. Medium-large blast radius. That answer tells her which guardrails she needs.

First she builds it in the sandbox, with a test key scoped only to send mail, and watches it draft and "send" to fake buyers across several weeks of test data until it never once addresses the wrong person or emails an unpaid order. Then she moves to real data but keeps the pipe on **draft, don't send** : every Monday it assembles twelve finished thank-yous in her voice, correctly skipping the unpaid orders using the `paid` box, and leaves them for her to glance at and release with two seconds of attention each. She reads the pipe's diary each week to confirm it drafted what it should have. And the one task she flatly refuses to automate, for now, is anything that _moves money_ , refunds especially, because that blast radius is the largest and she has decided the two minutes of doing a refund by hand is a fair price for keeping her own hand on it. She did not refuse the automation. She bounded it, exactly as far as its blast radius demanded, and no further.


### 12.6 Exercises

Read the answers.


#### Judgment scenario

**Q1.** Your assistant proposes: "To save you time, I'll automatically issue refunds to any customer who emails asking for one, right away, no need for you to review." Run the 3 a.m. question on this, name the blast radius, and redesign the pipe with the safe-posture set so it is still useful but bounded.

**Answer:** The 3 a.m. answer is alarming: misfiring, this pipe could issue unlimited refunds to anyone who sends a triggering email, including bad-faith or mistaken requests, with real money moving irreversibly and no natural limit, because a machine does not tire of refunding. That is a very large blast radius: irreversible _and_ money-touching _and_ triggerable by outsiders. Redesigned with the safe-posture set: build and prove it in the _sandbox_ first; give it a key scoped only to the refund power, nothing else; put a hard _spending cap_ at the service so total refunds can never exceed a number you chose while calm; and, most important, require your human "yes" before each payment (the irreversible-action gate), so it prepares a proposed refund for each request and leaves it for you to release rather than paying automatically. Now it saves Mara the drudgery of assembling each refund while keeping her hand on every irreversible payment. Useful, and bounded exactly to its danger.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 12: Handing the Agent the Keys
blocks.src:
#### Predict the posture

**Q2.** For each pipe, say roughly how much of the safe-posture set it needs, and why: (a) "Every morning, read my calendar and tell me my first meeting." (b) "Every Friday, post my week's new products to my public mailing list." (c) "Whenever inventory of a mug drops below five, automatically reorder clay supplies and pay for them."

**Answer:** (a) needs _almost none_ : it only reads, so its blast radius is tiny (worst case, it reads your calendar an extra time), and you can let it run freely. (b) needs _several_ : it _posts publicly and irreversibly_ to real people, so it wants a sandbox trial, and above all _draft-don't-send_ , a human "yes" before the week's post goes out, because a wrong or half-written post cannot be un-posted. (c) needs _all of them_ : it is irreversible _and_ spends real money _and_ runs unattended on a trigger, the largest kind of blast radius, so it needs sandbox proof, a narrowly scoped key, a hard spending cap, a readable diary, and almost certainly a draft-don't-send or human "yes" on the actual payment until it has earned deep trust. The pattern to carry: read little guarding, send more guarding, spend the most guarding, and the 3 a.m. question tells you which each pipe is.


#### Say this to your AI

This is the second load-bearing ask of the book, the one that makes acting-on-your-behalf safe by default.

> _"Before you ever run an automation that acts on the world on my behalf, walk me through the worst it could do if it misfired while I was asleep. Sort what it does into reversible things you can just do, and irreversible things, sending, posting, paying, deleting, that need my okay. Prove it in a sandbox with fake data first. For anything that costs money, set a hard spending cap I choose. For anything that messages real people, draft it and let me release it rather than sending it yourself. And keep a plain record of what you actually did each time, so I can check afterward. Don't hand me convenience by removing my hand from the things that can't be undone."_

This ask is the entire safe-posture set spoken in plain words: the 3 a.m. blast-radius question, the reversible-versus-irreversible sort, sandbox-first, spending caps, draft-don't-send, and a readable diary. Standing behind Chapter 6's key-hygiene ask, it is what lets you enjoy the book's whole promise, the boring work doing itself, without ever handing over more of yourself than the task requires. Say it once as a standing rule, and every acting pipe you build inherits it.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 12: Handing the Agent the Keys
blocks.src:
### Chapter Summary

This chapter crossed the line from an assistant that _describes and builds_ pipes to one that _acts_ through them, holding your keys and changing the world unattended, which is exactly why Chapter 6 mattered squared. The habit that governs the crossing is the **3 a.m. question** , given full ceremony here: _what is the worst this pipe could do if it misfired while I'm asleep?_ , whose answer is the pipe's **blast radius** , a map of where to place guardrails rather than a reason to refuse. Underneath sits the deepest cut, **reversible versus irreversible** : let the machine do freely the things that can be undone, and keep a human hand on the things that _send, post, pay,_ or _destroy_. The guardrails themselves are calm and concrete, the **safe-posture set** : test mode first, dry runs that preview irreversible steps, hard spending caps on anything that costs, and _draft, don't send_ for messages to real people, plus a readable **diary** of what the pipe actually did, so trust means _able to check_ rather than blind faith.

Here is a promise no honest map will make: that your automations, once built, will run forever untouched. They will not. This chapter is about that truth, and about why knowing it makes you _more_ capable rather than less.

Every automation is a small standing bet that the world will keep behaving the way it did the day you built it. But the world does not hold still. Services change under you. Keys expire. Formats shift. Free tiers shrink. A pipe that ran perfectly in March can quietly stop working in June because something on the other end moved. A book that hid this from you would be selling you a fantasy, and you would discover the truth alone, at the worst moment, wondering what you did wrong. You did nothing wrong. Pipes are fragile because the ground they stand on moves, and the mature question is not _will this break_ but _how will I know when it does, and what will I do?_


### 13.1 The as-of discipline, now for running things

Throughout this series there is a habit called the as-of discipline: the recognition that specific facts about services, their prices, their features, their exact shapes, are true only _as of_ a moment, and will drift. We have applied it to what this book says. Now apply it to what your _pipes_ do.

A running automation is a frozen snapshot of how services worked the day it was built. It assumes the shop's orders come back with a certain label, that the mail service accepts a certain kind of request, that a key stays valid, that a free tier stays free. Each of those is an as-of fact, true when you built the pipe, and each can change without warning, because the services owe you no promise to stay still. When one changes, the pipe's frozen assumption is now wrong, and the pipe misbehaves.

This is not a flaw in your building. It is the nature of building on ground you do not own. Every automation you commission is, in a real sense, a small ongoing relationship with services that will keep evolving, and part of owning a pipe is accepting that the relationship needs occasional maintenance. The pipe is not a monument you build once. It is a garden you tend.


### 13.2 The design question: how will I know?

Since pipes will break, the single most important thing you can build into one is not a way to never break. It is a way to _tell you when it has_.

Think about the difference between two failures. In the first, a pipe breaks loudly: it stops, it shows the honest "no" it hit, and it lets you know something is wrong. In the second, a pipe breaks _silently_ : it keeps running, but it is now doing the wrong thing, or nothing, and it never tells you, so you find out weeks later when a customer asks why they never got their thank-you note. The loud failure is a minor annoyance. The silent failure is the real danger, because the cost is not the breakage; it is all the time you spent trusting a pipe that had stopped deserving it.

So "how will I know it broke?" is a _design question_ you ask while building, not a problem you handle after. A well-built pipe is built to fail loudly: to notice when an answer arrives in the wrong shape or a step refuses, to stop rather than plow ahead, and to tell you. This is where the diary from Chapter 12 earns its keep again, and where a simple "let me know if this pipe fails" instruction is worth more than any amount of hoping. You cannot prevent breakage. You can absolutely decide, in advance, that breakage will announce itself instead of hiding.

#### Definition: Failing loudly

A pipe **fails loudly** when, on hitting a problem, it stops and tells you, rather than continuing to run while doing the wrong thing. Building a pipe to fail loudly, by checking that answers arrive in the expected shape, stopping on a refusal, and alerting you when something is off, is the single most valuable protection against the real danger of automation, which is not breakage but _silent_ breakage discovered too late.


### 13.3 Mara's format shift

Let us watch a pipe break, because seeing it done gracefully removes most of the dread.

One week, months into her smooth-running setup, Mara's shop service quietly changes how it hands back orders: the label her pipe relied on to read the buyer's name gets renamed, or the shipping box gets rearranged. The shop did not warn her; services rarely do. On Monday, her pipeline runs and something goes wrong. If Mara built it well, it fails _loudly_ : the pipe notices that the answer no longer has the shape it expected, stops, and tells her "the orders came back, but I couldn't find the buyer's name where I expected it." That message is a gift. It points straight at what changed.

Now the honest "no"s from Chapter 5 and the readable diary from Chapter 12 do their work together. Mara, or her assistant, looks at the actual response, sees that the label moved, and adjusts the pipe to read from the new location. Ten minutes, and the garden is tended. Compare the alternative: a pipe built to plow ahead silently would have kept "reading" orders with a blank where each buyer's name should be, drafting a dozen thank-you notes addressed to no one, and Mara would have learned about it from a confused customer, days later. Same breakage, wildly different cost, and the difference was entirely a design choice made in advance: fail loud, not silent.

This is why fragility, faced honestly, is not frightening. Mara's pipe broke, exactly as this chapter promised it would, and it was a minor Monday chore rather than a disaster, because she built it expecting to break and telling her when it did. The fragile pipe you understand and monitor is a completely different animal from the fragile pipe you trusted blindly.

### 13.4 When a manual step is honestly better

Here is a conclusion that a lesser book would never admit: sometimes the right answer is _not_ to automate at all, and knowing when is a mark of judgment, not defeat.

If a task is fragile in a way that would break constantly, if the service it depends on changes often, or the task is rare, or the two minutes of doing it by hand is genuinely less total effort than building and _maintaining_ a pipe that will keep breaking, then the honest move is to keep it manual. An automation that breaks every third week and needs your attention each time may cost you more than the chore ever did. The goal was never to automate everything; it was to spend your effort well. Sometimes spending it well means doing a small thing by hand and refusing to build a brittle machine to avoid it.

This connects back to Chapter 10's judgment about what deserves automating, but adds a maintenance-flavored test: not just "is this worth building?" but "is this worth _keeping running_?" A pipe that would demand constant repair fails the second test even if it passed the first. There is real dignity in a manual step chosen on purpose. The mature map-reader automates the durable, boring, repeated work and shrugs cheerfully at the fragile, occasional task, doing it by hand and losing no sleep.


### 13.5 The front door, not the window

One last honesty, and it is about _how_ you reach a service, because there is a tempting wrong path worth naming clearly.

Some services do not offer a counter window at all, or do not offer one for the thing you want. In that moment there is a temptation: have your assistant read the service's _human website_ instead, scraping the information off the page the way a person's eyes would, going around the front the service actually built. Resist this, at the gist level, for three honest reasons. First, it is _fragile_ in the extreme: a human website is decoration a machine has to guess through, and it changes constantly, so a pipe built on scraping breaks even more often than one built on a counter window. Second, it is _often, though not always, against the service's terms_ : many services explicitly ask you not to, so the honest move is to check what a service actually says rather than assume either way, and going around a door the service deliberately built can shade into taking without asking. Third, it is often _impolite_ , the automation equivalent of climbing through a window when a service left its counter closed on purpose.

The honest posture is: use the counter window, the front door the service built for machines, when it exists. When it does not, treat that as the service saying "not this way," and either find a service that does offer the door, or do the task by hand, rather than forcing your way through the human website. This is the ToS-honesty that keeps your automations both durable and decent. A map that showed you the window and called it a shortcut would be leading you into a swamp. This book shows you the front door and, when there is no front door, tells you honestly to walk.

#### Common Misconception

_"A good automation is one I build once and never think about again."_

That is a wish, not a description, and holding it is how people get burned. Automations live in a changing world and require occasional tending, so the good ones are not the untouched ones; they are the ones built to _tell you when they need tending_. Aiming for never-think-about-it-again leads you to build silent pipes and trust them blindly, which sets up the exact disaster this chapter warns about: a pipe that stopped working weeks ago and never said so. The realistic and better aim is a pipe that runs quietly when all is well and speaks up the moment it is not, so your attention is spent only when it is genuinely needed. Not "set it and forget it," but "set it and be told." That is the honest promise, and it is a better one.
